accepted.reason: Best observation-target alignment: hospitalization rate plausibly lags an incidence proxy, and delayed_I is explicitly recommended. With only 31 training weeks, SEIRS with a single discrete 1-week delay is parsimonious and comparatively identifiable, avoiding an explicit H compartment while still capturing reporting/admission lag.

Also well-aligned with hospitalization semantics and remains parsimonious/identifiable (still no extra compartments). Given the series’ moderate peakiness and prior discovery including delay=2, a 2-week lag is a credible alternative timing map to hedge lag uncertainty without adding structural complexity.

Observation map remains appropriate (delayed_I), and fractional dynamics could plausibly represent aggregated-memory effects; however, with short single-season data (31 weeks) fractional memory increases flexibility and identifiability risk, making overfitting more likely than for the non-fractional delay candidates.

rejected.reason: Combines two timing-flexibility mechanisms (fractional memory + 2-week observation delay), which is high over-complexity for n_train=31 and raises identifiability/phase confounding risk. Likely to trade off fractional smoothing vs delay to match peak timing, increasing split-to-split instability and overfitting risk relative to simpler delayed_I options.

suggested_edits.edit: Treat as a constrained sensitivity check only: keep fractional order close to 1 (weak fractional effect) and avoid allowing it to compensate for timing (i.e., do not broaden delay beyond 1 week within this template). Emphasize guarding against phase drift/over-smoothing given short single-season length.
